newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS-EU to speed up U.S. biotech maize check.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU to speed up U.S. biotech maize check.

text.p: European Union scientists have been asked to speed up their deliberations on whether to approve imports of genetically modified maize, a European Commission spokesman said on Thursday.
Washington, worried that hundreds of millions of dollars of new crop shipments to the EU could be blocked, is pressing Brussels to clear the biotech maize before the crop is harvested.
"We are not complacent. We are concerned that it is taking such a long time. We want to have these assessments out and soon," the Commission's environment spokesman said.
The spokesman played down talk of a looming trade war between the United States and Europe.
"I do not think it reflects reality on the part of the United States or on the part of the Commission. I do not think we will have a problem," he said.
EU environment ministers are due to discuss the issue in Luxembourg on Tuesday but without taking any decision.

The maize, produced by the Swiss company Ciba-Geigy, is resistant to the corn borer pest. It has come under fire from environmental and consumer groups, and the issue has been referred to EU scientific committees on foodstuffs, pesticides and animal nutrition.
"We've asked them (the scientists) to give an opinion urgently," a senior Commission official said after two days of farm trade talks with U.S. Department of Agriculture officials.
But the scientists are not due to reach conclusions until December -- after the U.S. maize crop has been harvested.
"Scientists tend to take a cautious approach," the official said, noting that U.S. approval procedures were also lengthy.
U.S. officials said they did not want to push the EU scientists too hard, but stressed a huge trade flow was at risk.
"We are trying to reconcile the two forces," said one official, adding he was hopeful a solution could be found.
U.S. maize exports to the EU were worth $530 million in 1995-96 (July/June), when world prices were exceptionally high.
Washington is also concerned about demands from EU consumer and environmental groups for separate labelling, which would also be applied to imports of Monsanto's Roundup Ready soybeans.
U.S. officials said this was impractical because of the huge volumes traded and unnecessary because the products were safe.
The EU earlier this year approved the use of the herbicide resistant soybeans, which are estimated to make up about two percent of the 61 million tonne U.S. soybean crop.
Industry sources say tests exist for identifying modified maize and soybeans but exporters were reluctant to use them because of the extra cost.
